data.title: Ecommerce Trends: How Lowe's is using AI
data.description:
Lowe’s Companies Inc. made artificial intelligence (AI) a priority in a wave of new Lowe’s executive promotions for September.

Its list of changes included adding AI to the formal title of Seemantini Godbole, Lowe’s chief information officer. And the value the home improvement retailer places on its AI tools spans both its consumer and Pro business segments.

Godbole summarized a few of the places internally that the retailer’s AI ambitions touch, following the Lowe’s 2026 Tech Fair, an annual showcase of the company’s technology projects.

“I could say so much about the tech we build, from our homegrown virtualization platform, to security anomaly detection, to our AI Foundry, to the many customer and associate facing products, our award winning Lowe’s app, and MyRedVest, our super popular product for store associates!” Godbole wrote on LinkedIn in September.

As Lowe’s online sales demonstrated in its latest Q2 earnings results, AI assistance appears to be having a material impact on key metrics.

How Lowe’s is using its Mylow AI assistant

“In fact, the conversion rate for online customers who use Mylow is triple that of customers who do not use the tool, reinforcing that a well-designed agentic AI experience can be a clear driver in the purchasing decision,” said Marvin Ellison, president, CEO and chairman at Lowe’s, during its August earnings call with investors.

Ellison noted during the call that Mylow, which is part of a larger app for Lowe’s associates, “has supported over 25 million questions from customers and associates” since it debuted in 2025.

Lowe’s crafted the Mylow assistant with the help of OpenAI. At the time, the retailer framed it as a way to expand engagement with its customers, both directly and as an aid through the Mylow Companion interface for staff as they assist shoppers.

Lowe’s ranks No. 9 in Digital Commerce 360’s Top 1000 Database. The market research tool tracks North America’s largest online retailers by their annual ecommerce sales.

Lowe’s is No. 90 in Digital Commerce 360’s all-new AI Rankings. That set of rankings is available in the Top 1000 Pro with AI Database.

Lowe’s web sales by year

What is the Lowe’s AI Foundry?

Lowe’s AI Foundry, which Godbole mentioned, is an integrated development environment (IDE) that the company established for work on AI-powered tools. It’s where internal development happens with guardrails in place for testing, with access to large language models (LLMs) for building out software, Lowe’s shared previously.

As the company tests new applications there, it can track performance and judge how technology may perform in real-world environments before deployments.

Why Lowe’s launched Materials Lists for Pro customers

In May, Lowe’s rolled out Materials Lists, an AI tool aimed at its Pro customers to help them take files and physical documents and integrate them into their planning process for faster turnaround times when receiving quotes.

“We know time is one of the most valuable resources for Pros, and every minute spent manually building estimates or organizing material lists is time taken away from serving customers and growing their businesses,” said Quonta Vance, executive vice president of Pro and home services at Lowe’s. “Material Lists is part of our broader commitment to building smarter, faster solutions that simplify the customer journey and help Pros save time, work more efficiently and stay competitive.”

Joseph McFarland, executive vice president of stores at Lowe’s, highlighted Materials Lists’ impact during the retailer’s May earnings call.

“Pros can bring in the list in just about any format, whether a photo, handwritten note, PDF or spreadsheet, and our associates can use this tool to convert it into an actionable quote,” McFarland stated. “In the past, this was a manual task, which meant generating these quotes could take days, taking associates away from serving Pro customers. Now, with this AI-enabled tool, we’ve reduced that time from days to minutes.”

In the current environment where Pro and online sales are driving growth amid macro challenges for consumers, Lowe’s ability to improve its Pro experience remains as important as ever.

data.title: Neighborhood Intelligence, F9 Brands end acquisition agreement
data.description:
Neighborhood Intelligence — the company that rebranded from Bed Bath & Beyond Inc. — and F9 Brands have ended their acquisition agreement. 

In April, Bed Bath & Beyond Inc. had planned to acquire F9 Brands’ assets as part of a $150 million deal. The acquisition would have included $37 million in cash and about 16 million shares of Bed Bath & Beyond stock at $7 per share. It would have seen Bed Bath & Beyond acquire brands to expand its services surrounding storage, closets, cabinets, flooring, installation, renovation and distribution.

In August, Bed Bath & Beyond Inc. announced it would rebrand to Neighborhood Intelligence. It began trading under that name on Aug. 17, using the ticker NXH on the Nasdaq as of that day.

Neighborhood Intelligence ranks No. 99 in Digital Commerce 360’s Top 1000 Database. The market research tool tracks North America’s largest online retailers by their annual ecommerce sales.

Neighborhood Intelligence is No. 307 in Digital Commerce 360’s all-new AI Rankings. That set of rankings falls under the Top 1000 Pro with AI Database.

Why Neighborhood Intelligence and F9 Brands are canceling their acquisition deal

In a Sept. 8 statement that Neighborhood Intelligence released, the retailer said it determined F9 Brands did not satisfy the closing requirements for the acquisition “within the contemplated timeframe.”

“Neighborhood will not proceed with the acquisition or enter into a commercial or strategic collaboration with F9,” the statement said. “The companies will continue to operate independently, and the terms and economics of the previously announced acquisition agreement are no longer in effect.”

The Housewares & Home Furnishings retail operator said as of Aug. 31, after completing other recent acquisitions, Neighborhood Intelligence had issued about 97 million shares of common stock. It said it will not issue shares or acquisition capital in connection with F9 Brands.

In the past year, Neighborhood Intelligence has acquired The Container Store, Kirkland’s, Installed Right and SFV Construction Services.

“Disciplined capital allocation and protecting shareholder value are central to how we evaluate every transaction,” said Marcus Lemonis, executive chairman of Neighborhood Intelligence, in the statement. “We evaluate opportunities continuously, and this is one of many transactions we have considered that we elected not to pursue.”

He added that Neighborhood Intelligence remains focused on strengthening its Home Services platform. That segment of its business includes Elfa, Closet Works and SFV Construction Services.

Neighborhood Intelligence said it plans to build on Elfa’s whole-home solutions platform. It seeks to leverage Elfa’s design, engineering and manufacturing capabilities across kitchen, laundry, bath, closet and garage segments.

Recent Neighborhood Intelligence acquisitions

Before the rebrand to Neighborhood Intelligence, Bed Bath & Beyond had acquired Installed Right and SFV Services, a 20-year-old company for construction and facilities management projects. The acquisition, which Bed Bath & Beyond announced in June, expanded the retailer’s capabilities surrounding installation, renovation, construction and project execution.

Bed Bath & Beyond had also reached a deal in April to acquire The Container Store. The $150 million deal also included Elfa and Closet Works.

Neighborhood Intelligence’s portfolio also includes the Bed Bath & Beyond retail brand, Overstock, and Buy Buy Baby.

Those acquisitions followed name changes, ownership changes and investments Bed Bath & Beyond made in 2025.

data.title: Sephora plans exclusive drops for TikTok Shop
data.description:
Beauty retailer Sephora is debuting on TikTok Shop, launching a new “Sephora Drop Shop” experience that turns product launches into monthly livestreamed events featuring celebrity hosts, brand founders and creator content.

Piloting in the U.S. starting Sept. 19, the format is geared to resonate on TikTok’s beauty-heavy social video platform. Sephora will hope to convert TikTok’s highly engaged audience there into shoppers through curated, exclusive drops rather than traditional product listings.

Sephora falls under parent company LVMH, which is No. 2 in the Europe Database. The market research tool tracks that region’s largest online retailers, ranking them by annual ecommerce sales and more.

Why Sephora is launching on TikTok Shop

Sephora outlined its TikTok Shop plans as part of a strategy to reach younger consumers and emerging beauty shoppers.

“TikTok Shop is a powerful extension of our global digital strategy and our commitment to meeting clients wherever they discover beauty,” said Anca Marola, global chief digital officer at Sephora.

Marola described Sephora’s approach as a test-and-learn mindset. It intends to watch how customers respond and see what drives sales.

“We are not only scaling our retailtainment model in the US, but also gathering critical insights to inform our digital innovation and future rollout across our global network,” Marola stated.

The company noted that beauty is TikTok’s most searched category, generating over a billion beauty-related searches each month. The initiative expands Sephora’s social commerce efforts as consumers increasingly discover beauty products through creator content and short-form video.

“Beauty discovery has always been core to Sephora’s ethos, and the rise of social commerce and digital marketplaces have reinforced the need to evolve how we engage with our beauty lovers,” said Artemis Patrick, CEO of Sephora North America, in a statement. “We already have an incredibly active beauty community on TikTok, so we are excited to take the next step and pilot the Sephora Drop Shop on TikTok Shop.”

How Sephora will use its TikTok Shop presence

“This platform gives us a new way to interact with our existing customers, while extending our reach to a highly immersed beauty audience,” Patrick said. “Importantly, the launch signifies a natural progression in how we continue to lead and innovate in beauty retail.”

Each of Sephora’s product drops will include teasers, interactive experiences and creator-led content, according to the retailer. It wants consumers to guess the brand in the spotlight.

Sephora said its experience will culminate in an official TikTok Live with a celebrity host, brand founders and creators. Together, they will:

  • Unveil featured products.
  • Answer audience questions.
  • Engage with viewers in real time.
  • Display products available for purchase.

“We’re thrilled to welcome Sephora to TikTok Shop,” said Bianca Sing, global head of strategic brand partnerships at TikTok Shop. “This launch brings together Sephora’s leadership in beauty discovery and curation with TikTok Shop’s unique ability to inspire and connect communities through entertainment, creators, culture and commerce.”

TikTok Shop’s potential for Sephora

Those who’ve built businesses on TikTok Shop said its retail/entertainment model has real staying power if brands execute it right.

Skip Chapman, founder of KAFX Body, a New Jersey-based personal-care manufacturer that operates in a similar space to Sephora, said the concept can definitely work.

“We grew heavily through TikTok Shop and live selling, have sold more than 80,000 deodorants, worked with thousands of affiliates, and at one point roughly 80% of our sales came through TikTok,” Chapman said.

He added that livestream shopping can convert, but only when the live presentation gives people a reason to stay and buy. If it feels like a commercial, he sees people continue to scroll.

“The advantage is that customers can ask a question, see the product demonstrated, and get an answer immediately,” Chapman assessed. “You are removing objections at the exact moment someone is deciding whether to buy.”

How TikTok Shop compares to traditional ecommerce experiences

Chapman noted that the Sephora Drop Shop model can work because it treats TikTok Shop differently from a traditional ecommerce site.

“The combination of a scheduled drop, exclusivity, creator content, and a live event builds anticipation and gives shoppers a reason to act now,” he said. “Scarcity may bring people in, but useful demonstrations and real interaction are what turn attention into sales.”

Chapman sees the most valuable parts of live selling happening beyond the orders placed during the stream.

“You hear customer objections, questions and reactions in real time,” he stated. “That feedback can shape future content, product pages, merchandising and even product development.”

Chapman described live sessions as both sales channels and customer research sessions.

“I expect retailtainment to grow, especially in beauty,” he said. “Beauty products often need demonstration, education, and trust before someone buys.”

How effective will TikTok Shop drops be for Sephora?

Eli Goodman, CEO and co-founder of Datos, a clickstream data and consumer insights company, characterized this new dedicated drop model on TikTok Shop as a smart next step for a brand that already lives where its customers discover products.

“Sephora partnering with TikTok is also a great example of a retailer applying streaming-platform logic to shopping, and it is wise of them to deliver exclusive items in a recurring cadence,” Goodman said.

Still, Goodman expects that this type of retail entertainment will have its limits.

“While this kind of format is great at getting eyeballs and gives retailers a reason to show up in someone’s feed repeatedly, it is still mostly a top-of-funnel play for most brands,” Goodman said.

Specifically, he noted that converting viewers into shoppers depends on how fast the content earns attention.

Converting on TikTok

“Brands need to hook ’em, and they’ve got to hook ’em fast,” Goodman said.

Datos clickstream research shows purchase decisions, especially in beauty, don’t end at checkout.

“In one Sephora customer journey we mapped, a shopper who’d already bought a foundation kept coming back to TikTok, reviews, and AI tools after the purchase to validate she’d picked the right shade,” Goodman said.

He emphasized that this customer behavior conveys that trust and validation don’t stop after a livestream ends.

“Brands need to optimize for post-purchase follow-through and shouldn’t just optimize for the live moment,” Goodman said.

He surmised the novelty will wear off fairly fast, but he also thinks the value will remain for shoppers and brands.

“Brands that treat retailtainment as a relationship/community channel, and not just a sales event, will find creative new ways to truly capture and convert customers,” Goodman said.

data.title: Rugs Direct adds AI assistant Ask Cleo for site search, PDP support
data.description:
Rugs Direct has rolled out its on-site AI-powered conversational assistant, Ask Cleo, and it’s driving increases in key performance indicators.

The retailer falls under Elevated Brands Group, also the parent company Lightopia. Elevated Brands Group launched Ask Cleo as separate rollouts for each retailer. Lightopia debuted Ask Cleo on its site in May, with Rugs Direct following weeks later, in early June.

Sharon Gautschi, chief merchandising officer of Elevated Brands Group, shared that since then, add-to-cart rates for consumers using Ask Cleo have been 8x to 9x more than other users across both Rugs Direct and Lightopia.

“But you do have to temper that with engagement,” Gautschi told Digital Commerce 360. “Certainly, the majority of customers are still using classic search. So that is a higher add-to-cart rate, but on a smaller base. We’re still ramping up engagement.”

Using agentic AI to power its search, Ask Cleo allows shoppers to describe what they are looking for conversationally. It can ask clarifying questions and help solve practical design challenges such as selecting an appropriate fixture for a vaulted ceiling, according to Elevated Brands Group.

Rugs Direct is No. 622 in the Top 1000 Database. The market research tool tracks North America’s largest online retailers, ranking them by annual ecommerce sales and more.

Rugs Direct is also No. 492 in Digital Commerce 360’s new AI Rankings. That set of rankings is available in the Top 1000 Pro with AI Database.

How Rugs Direct and Lightopia are using AI agents for search

Consumer shopping both Rugs Direct and Lightopia are “really showing us that they are looking for quality,” Gautschi said. But there’s another set of customers chasing fashion, she added.

“They are clearly interested in using conversational or natural language search,” Gautschi explained. “And that’s becoming more and more prevalent across our industry, which is exciting and fun. They really want more answers, they want it fast and they want to understand the results.”

She shared that Elevated Brands Group tapped Constructor to develop Ask Cleo. Lightopia and Rugs Direct both use Ask Cleo in two different ways:

  • AI Shopping Assistant (ASA). Gautschi described this as a site-level or higher-funnel search tool.
  • Product Insights Agent (PIA). She described this tool as living on a product’s page to answer specific questions about it.

“Overall, we’ve seen some interesting trends where the more questions they ask, then the higher the KPIs are,” Gautschi said. “The signals are stronger. We’re seeing higher add-to-cart, higher purchase rates.”

Consumers on Rugs Direct might use Ask Cleo to learn about a rug’s materials, thickness and dimensions, she noted. On Lightopia’s site, they might use Ask Cleo more spec-focused questions, she said, as lighting is “much more technical” than rugs. That could mean asking about dimmability, ceiling height, bulb compatibility or color temperature.

How Elevated Brands Group trained its AI agent

Gautschi said Elevated Brands Group plays “a big part” in feeding information to train its AI agent. Elevated Brands Group has articles and blog posts that it has written for public relations and search engine optimization (SEO). It also has specifications for all its products.

Elevated Brands Group has taken that library of content and given it to Ask Cleo, according to Gautschi. The training process took about four to six weeks, she estimated. Ultimately, though, it comes down to bandwidth.

She also praised the company’s emphasis on data integrity.

“Even some of the larger companies I’ve worked with, getting one spec updated across my assortment is really hard, but here, we’re pretty nimble with data integrity,” Gautschi said. “And that’s able to feed the agents quite well, where the agents can really respond nicely.”

Using all that data, Rugs Direct and Lightopia have trained Ask Cleo on brand voice and how they want it to respond to consumers. Gautschi said the company intends for the Ask Cleo tool to function like a “well-informed friend with great design, style and taste.”

“It doesn’t just say, here’s what you want,” according to Gautschi. “It really should give you some advice and some additional things to think about for what you’re looking for. We feed it and then we test it, so we’ll ask it questions to see how it responds. And if it doesn’t respond in a way that we think is right — or the answer can be optimized — then we are giving those examples back to our third party.”

Off-site AI traffic to Lightopia, Rugs Direct

Gautschi noted that Rugs Direct and Lightopia are increasingly generating traffic from AI platforms such as OpenAI’s ChatGPT, Anthropic’s Claude, or Perplexity. She estimated that AI traffic referrals generate less than 10% of consumers’ visits to the two retailers’ sites.

“We are definitely getting more traffic from AI platforms, but not enough,” Gautschi said. “I want more. And as a smaller company — we’re not Wayfair, we’re not Walmart — we’re competing with those big guys. We’re definitely seeing the traffic come our way, and we have nowhere to go but up, fortunately, in terms of increasing that traffic.”

That growth in traffic could also help bring visibility to the online retailers’ Ask Cleo tool. If agentic AI-powered search platforms’ traffic becomes “more qualified,” she said, then Elevated Brands Group will expect return on investment (ROI) and return on ad spend (ROAS) to be higher than traditional digital paid marketing programs.

data.title: Instacart launches AI assistant Clementine, agentic commerce integrations
data.description:
Instacart has launched an artificial intelligence assistant, Clementine, for grocery shopping support while adding new partners for its existing enterprise AI tool Cart Assistant.

As of Sept. 9, Instacart users in North America can tap Clementine for “the hardest parts of grocery shopping,” according to the company. It referred to decisions such as what to make for a meal, “shopping the way a family actually eats” and staying within budget. Instacart said the AI assistant helps users develop a personalized cart in seconds. It added that it based the Clementine experience on “what’s actually available on shelves in real time from the customer’s chosen store, so people can spend less time figuring out what’s for dinner and more time actually enjoying it.”

Chris Rogers, CEO at Instacart, said in a statement that millions of families ask themselves what’s for dinner on a given night. They don’t know the answer or what to shop for, he added.

“We’ve spent nearly 15 years learning how families shop and eat, and Clementine puts that knowledge to work,” Rogers said. “It learns from the preferences you share and the way you’ve shopped on Instacart. It can help you stay on budget and surface what’s actually in stock at your chosen store, handling enough of the weekly planning that the mental load actually feels lighter.”

Instacart said early results show that its customers start with tasks such as restocking before using the AI tool for “higher-order use cases,” such as recipe discovery.

On average, Instacart said, customers placing orders through the Clementine AI assistant include more items than other users. Those customers using Clementine tend to also exceed $115 in average order value, according to Instacart.

How the Instacart Clementine AI assistant works

Instacart said its Clementine AI assistant factors in data from more than 1.6 billion lifetime orders and a catalog of more than 2 billion items. Additionally, Instacart said, Clementine uses more than 10 million daily inventory signals from about 100,000 locations across 2,200 retail operators in North America.

According to Instacart, that foundation powers its inventory intelligence, allowing the Clementine AI to understand what products are available in real time as well as what’s on sale at any given moment.

Instacart said its Clementine AI assistant can:

  • generate personalized recipes and display curated existing options
  • make suggestions based on a household’s dietary restrictions and preferences
  • help customers find deals and promotions, as well as lower-cost alternatives
  • reorder automatically
  • create occasion-centered shopping lists
  • upload grocery lists, whether handwritten or digital screenshots, converting them into lists of products to add to cart

“Grocery shopping is one of the most routine things people do, and also one of the most personal,” said John Adams, vice president and head of product at Instacart, in a statement. “What we built with Clementine is a system that understands both of those things — not just what you need, but how you eat, what you love, and what’s on the shelves at your store right now. Whatever you’re craving or planning for, Clementine can get you there. The more you use it, the more it feels like a natural part of how your household shops, becoming something you reach for week after week.”

Instacart adds partners for white-label AI tool Cart Assistant

In addition to Clementine, Instacart offers what it describes as a white-label AI tool, Cart Assistant. It said that tool is “for grocers who want to offer their own branded agentic shopping experience on their website and app.”

Instacart said the Cart Assistant combines its grocery data with a retailer’s catalog and customer data. That helps it to create a branded assistant that can suggest relevant deals and recipes. At the same time, it helps users to build carts without searching for products item by item. The company said grocers can customize the name, tone, loyalty integration and recipe content.

Instacart said current retailers using Cart Assistant include Food Bazaar, Heritage Grocers Group and Woodman’s. It said Harmon’s, The Save Mart, Stew Leonard’s and more companies will follow.

Additionally, Instacart said it has partnered with Anthropic, OpenAI and Google. It said grocery conversations that begin on Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini or AI Mode in Google Search “can be seamlessly completed on Instacart, where users can place an order from their preferred retailer for delivery or pickup.”
